extracted.intended_audience: employers, regulated entities, labor lawyers, economists, researchers, and public commenters on the Department of Labor's independent-contractor/FLSA rulemaking
extracted.subtask_description: Economic analysis and supporting methodological standards used by the Department of Labor to estimate prevalence, costs, benefits, and impacts of the final independent-contractor rule under the FLSA. Includes data-source selection, bias treatment, cost calculation assumptions, and response to public comments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency with longstanding judicial precedent / economic reality test
rubrics_metrics.description: The rule adopts guidance essentially identical to the standard the Department applied for decades prior to the 2021 IC Rule, derived from the same analysis that courts have applied for decades and have been continuing to apply since the 2021 IC Rule took effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This alignment with judicial precedent is intended to provide employers and workers with guidance consistent with long-standing case law and to reduce misclassification and legal disputes. The Department contrasts this approach with the 2021 IC Rule's elevation of certain factors and preclusion of consideration of relevant facts under several factors, which the Department says departed from judicial precedent and could have increased misclassification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not apply ABC test reclassification estimates to this rule
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department's economic reality test is not the ABC test; therefore, reclassification or job-loss estimates associated with a nationwide ABC test are not appropriate to apply to this rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commenters cited studies modeling an ABC test (e.g., study projecting large job losses); the Department explains those studies examine the 'ABC Test' and thus cannot be applied to its economic reality test and are excluded from the estimated impacts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use CPS Contingent Worker Supplement (CWS) as the lower-bound estimate of independent contractors
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department believes the Current Population Survey (CPS) Contingent Worker Supplement offers an appropriate lower bound for the number of independent contractors because it is nationally representative and has a large sample.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CWS measures those who say their independent contractor job is their primary job and that they worked at that job in the survey's reference week (10.6 million in 2017, 6.9 percent). The Department notes potential biases in the CWS (single-week reference, proxy responses, self-identification issues) and documents these limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adjust CWS primary-job estimate to include secondary/occasional independent contracting
rubrics_metrics.description: Integrate estimated proportions of workers who are independent contractors on secondary or otherwise excluded jobs to produce an estimate population of 22.1 million independent contractors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example methodology: apply research (Lim et al. or others) indicating that independent contracting work is the primary source of income for 48 percent of independent contractors; dividing the CWS primary-job estimate (10.6 million) by 0.48 yields 22.1 million. Department presents alternative estimates and explains why it did not adopt some state- or single-state surveys to adjust the estimate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify and document data-source biases; do not quantitatively adjust absent reliable bias magnitudes
rubrics_metrics.description: Potential biases in primary data sources include single-week reference undercounting, proxy responses, respondents misidentifying status, informal work not self-identified, and misclassification by employers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department reviews evidence (e.g., RAND ALP vs CWS differences, Abraham et al. findings) and concludes that reliable data on the magnitude and net direction of these biases are unavailable; therefore, it does not attempt to quantify how these biases impact the estimated number of independent contractors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider range of literature and prefer sources with larger sample sizes or recent data for primary estimates
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department conducted a literature review (e.g., CPS CWS, RAND ALP, Gallup, GSS QWL, Jackson et al., Lim et al.) and chose sources with larger sample sizes and/or more recent data for the primary estimate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Table 1 summarizes the various methods and findings. The Department excluded some studies from the primary estimate when they were limited to one state, broader populations, or non-U.S. workers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use tax data estimates as complementary evidence with specified pros and cons
rubrics_metrics.description: Studies using tax data (Jackson et al., Lim et al.) are considered; these tend to show increases over time but require inferring independent-contractor status from filings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advantages of tax data: large samples, year-round activity records, reduced reporting bias, inclusion of primary and secondary contractors. Disadvantages: need to infer status (IRS definitions differ from FLSA), likely underreporting bias, inclusion of misclassified workers, and lack of publicly available detailed source data for verification and adjustment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate and document COVID-19 related changes but avoid unwarranted adjustments when evidence is inconclusive
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department searched for recent data to indicate trends since 2017; findings (e.g., SHED, MBO Partners) are inconclusive and generally do not indicate a clear increase, so no adjustment to the 2017-based estimate was made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department notes some surveys show decreases (2017 to 2020), some increases in 2021 for 'occasional independents', and that changes in survey questions limit comparability. Commenter-cited Upwork estimates were judged likely to use broader definitions and the sample representativeness could not be verified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demographic and industry characterization using CWS primary-job data with caveats
rubrics_metrics.description: Use CWS to report demographics (age, sex, race, industry, education) of primary independent contractors (e.g., more prevalent in construction and professional/business services; 64% male; age differences across generations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department notes that CWS only measures primary-job independent contractors and other surveys capturing secondary or informal work may show different patterns (e.g., informal work more prevalent among younger ages, racial minorities). The analysis explicitly flags limitations when inferring demographic shifts post-COVID.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define universe for regulatory familiarization costs using establishments plus government entities
rubrics_metrics.description: To estimate establishments incurring familiarization costs, the Department used Statistics of U.S. Businesses (SUSB) plus Census of Government counts to define a universe of 8,049,229 establishments and government entities, then restricted to establishments that engage independent contractors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department chooses establishments (rather than firms) because regulatory familiarization plausibly occurs at headquarters and establishment levels; it then applies an estimated share of establishments that hire contractors (35 percent) from Lim et al. to arrive at 2.8 million entities subject to familiarization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select reviewer occupation and compute effective hourly cost with benefits and overhead
rubrics_metrics.description: Assume a Compensation, Benefits, and Job Analysis Specialist (SOC 13-1141) will review the rule; use median wage $32.59 (2022), add benefits at 45% and overhead at 17% to compute an effective hourly rate of $52.80.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This occupational selection and cost-computation method aligns with prior Wage and Hour Division rules (including 2021 IC Rule). The Department acknowledges commenter concerns that higher-paid staff may review the rule but defends the use of this occupation as consistent with precedent and prior rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assumed time-per-reviewer: 1 hour for establishments, 0.5 hour for independent contractors (updated from proposed rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department estimates on average about 1 hour for establishment reviewers (previously 30 minutes in proposed rule) and 30 minutes (0.5 hour) for independent contractors (previously 15 minutes), increased in response to commenters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department doubled earlier estimates after receiving comments that the original times were understated. It justifies the final averages by noting many establishments rely on third-party summaries or spend little/no time reviewing the rule, and independent contractors are likely to rely on summaries as well.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value independent contractors' familiarization time using median CWS wage updated to 2022 dollars
rubrics_metrics.description: Time for independent contractors is valued at $23.46 per hour, derived from the CWS median hourly wage of $19.45 updated to 2022 dollars using the GDP deflator.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applying 0.5 hour per independent contractor and the 22.1 million estimate yields the independent-contractor portion of regulatory familiarization costs; the Department explains why the IC hourly valuation differs from establishment reviewer valuation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compute total one-time familiarization costs and annualize over 10 years with discount rates
rubrics_metrics.description: Total one-time regulatory familiarization costs are estimated at $408 million (establishments + independent contractors). Annualized 10-year costs are $56.4 million at a 3% discount rate or $54.3 million at a 7% discount rate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department treats familiarization as a one-time cost, assuming de minimis costs in future years because employers and contractors would continue to familiarize themselves with the legal framework absent the rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish transfers from costs in cost accounting
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain commenter-identified impacts (e.g., employer provision of health insurance and benefits, indirect higher taxes) are considered transfers rather than net resource costs and are discussed separately (e.g., section VII.E), not double-counted as compliance costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department notes transfers are treated differently from resource costs in its economic analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for potential ongoing compliance activities in stakeholder comments, but limit cost inclusion where reclassification is not expected to be widespread
rubrics_metrics.description: Commenters described additional potential costs (individualized assessments, renegotiation of contracts, tracking hours/pay, engagement with unions, enforcement responses). The Department recognizes these possible compliance burdens but states it does not expect widespread reclassification and that good practice already includes assessing economic relationships.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department responds that for limited cases where reclassification occurs, some of these costs may already be incurred; however, it documents commenters' claims and explains its reasoning for excluding or limiting certain estimated costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat reduced misclassification and increased consistency as benefits
rubrics_metrics.description: The rule's codification of judicial precedent and its detailed economic-reality analysis are expected to provide clearer guidance, increase consistency in classification decisions, and thereby reduce misclassification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department frames improved public understanding and reduced legal disputes as benefits; labor organizations argued rule will improve public understanding and lower compliance costs by codifying precedent in an accessible format.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respond to public comments by revising assumptions or explaining rationale
rubrics_metrics.description: Where commenters raised substantive objections (e.g., time-to-review, choice of reviewer occupation, alternative prevalence estimates), the Department either adjusted assumptions (doubled review times) or provided reasoned explanations why other suggestions were not adopted (e.g., Upwork study's broader freelancer definition, representativeness concerns).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The rule documents specific commenter claims, cites examples, and explains the Department's reasoned acceptance, partial acceptance, or rejection of those claims in the economic analysis.
